transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2026-03-26 16:00 UTC
Duration: 48 minutes
Attendees: Jordan Patel (Redwood AE), Maya Chen (Redwood SE), Luis Romero (Redwood SA); Ethan Clarke, Priya Menon, Liam O'Neill, Sara Kim (Orion Capital)

[00:00] Jordan (Redwood AE): hey everyone, thanks for carving out time, really appreciate it. quick agenda — understand your workloads, talk about per-token economics, and surface levers like batching, kv caching, dedicated capacity, and then agree next steps.

[00:22] Ethan (Orion): yeah, thanks. i'll be brief — we're exploring Redwood because we need consistent inference costs for two projects: an internal research assistant used by analysts and a lower-latency trading signal pipeline. budget sanity is top of mind — Liam here will ask the money questions.

[00:37] Liam (VP Finance): hi — yep. two numbers: we have a target of roughly $40k/month dedicated budget initially, may expand if unit costs justify. we need to understand per-token forward costs and predictable ceilings.

[00:50] Maya (Redwood SE): cool, that's super helpful. quick clarifying q — what's your expected traffic shape? steady queries or big bursts?

[01:00] Priya: research assistant is a moderate steady load, peaks during market open. avg prompt ~120 tokens, avg response ~400 tokens. qps about 15 steady, bursts up to 120 for hourly reports. trading signal pipeline is low-latency single-turn queries, avg 60 tokens in/out, but strict 200ms latency SLO.

[01:30] Jordan: perfect. that distribution matters a lot for batching and caching effectiveness. our hosted pricing is per-input+output token with volume breakpoints; dedicated brings lower per-token costs because you're reserving capacity and benefiting from packing and continuous KV cache.

[01:50] Ethan: when you say per-token, what's the ballpark? we saw some numbers on your site but need concrete examples that map to our traffic.

[02:02] Maya: high level, hosted gen endpoints start at around $0.0008 per token for large open models in the entry tier and can go down with volume. dedicated reserved capacity can drop to ~$0.0003-0.0005 per token depending on model family and commit. these are example ranges — we'll send your team a spreadsheet with line items.

[02:25] Liam: that delta is big — how realistic is the drop to $0.0003? what's driving that?

[02:33] Luis (Redwood SA): it's driven by fixed-cost amortization of GPU pools, better packing (more tokens per GPU-hour), continuous KV cache saving repeated prefixes, and custom quantization profiles that let you run cheaper variants while keeping quality.

[02:50] Sara (Security): quick interruption — any difference in data residency or audit logs between hosted and dedicated? if we move PII through the research assistant we need auditability and KMS control.

[03:05] Jordan: good call. hosted has SOC2, audit logs, and optional VPC peering; dedicated gives you stronger isolation and can be deployed in a private VPC with customer-managed KMS for encryption-in-use and at-rest. private/on-prem is the most controlled but higher TCO.

[03:30] Ethan: okay, about batching — you mentioned latency tradeoffs. the trading team won't accept 200ms to spike higher because of batching. how do we balance that?

[03:44] Maya: right. batching improves GPU utilization and reduces per-token cost but increases tail latency. our routing rules let you split traffic: route latency-sensitive queries to a low-latency pool (smaller batch sizes, guaranteed p99 targets) and route background/analytics to a high-throughput pool with larger batching.

[04:05] Priya: so effectively we can have a hybrid routing policy? some on hosted low-latency and others on dedicated?

[04:12] Luis: exactly. we often see customers put front-office latency-critical paths on dedicated small instances or on a high-tier hosted route with reserved capacity. background jobs run on cheaper dedicated or spot capacity. plus we support automatic fallback to cheaper model variants if primary is busy.

[04:28] Liam: model variants — is that like smaller models or quantized versions? how does that affect quality?

[04:35] Maya: both. we have curated model variants and quantized builds. quantization can reduce memory and increase throughput, dropping costs. quality impact depends on the model and your prompts; we'll run evals on your prompt set. typical tradeoffs are tiny for retrieval-augmented prompts but more visible for creative generation.

[04:58] Ethan: can caching help with cost for the research assistant? a lot of our analysts run similar queries.

[05:05] Maya: yes — prefix/KV caching is huge for reuse. with a high cache hit rate, you avoid re-computing early layers and dramatically reduce per-token compute. caching effectiveness is driven by prompt repetition and session behavior. if your analyst templates repeat prefixes, you could see cost cut by 20-60% on those flows.

[05:28] Priya: what's the work to enable KV cache? is it a config flag or model change?

[05:34] Luis: mostly config and SDK usage. you need to use the session API patterns — preserve session IDs, reuse KV tokens. there are some constraints on maximum cache sizes and eviction policies which we can tune per workload.

[05:50] Liam: back to numbers — can you give an example monthly estimate showing hosted baseline vs dedicated with caching and batching? assume our 15 qps steady research assistant with the prompt/response sizes i mentioned and trading being 100 qps bursts but low average.

[06:05] Maya: sure — high level example, approximate, not a quote: hosted (no caching) — for those token sizes and 15 qps steady, you might be looking at $30k-50k/month. With dedicated and moderate commit plus caching you'd be down to $12k-22k/month for the research assistant. Trading low-latency pool (small dedicated) might be an incremental $6k-10k. Combined you're in that $18k-32k range depending on cache hit rates and batch efficiency.

[06:40] Ethan: that aligns with our budget target if we hit the lower end. what's needed to lock in those dedicated numbers? commit duration and size?

[06:48] Jordan: typically a 6-12 month reserved commitment with throughput targets. we model commitments vs overage. we'll show scenarios: smaller commit with burst credits vs larger commit with lower unit price.

[07:05] Priya: in terms of benchmarking — how do we validate latency for trading? we'd want to run a 24-72 hour pilot with our traffic shape.

[07:13] Maya: absolutely. we'd run a benchmark: provide us with prompt set and token distributions, we'll spin up a mirror environment (dedicated or hosted reserved) and run against your workloads, measuring p50/p95/p99 and cost per token. recommend a 48-hour run to capture diurnal patterns.

[07:30] Sara: security follow-up — we need SOC2 report, encryption at rest with our KMS, SSO via SAML, and detailed audit logs. can you share those?

[07:39] Jordan: yes, we'll share SOC2 artifact, our architecture for KMS integration, and sample audit log formats. for dedicated/private we can support customer-managed KMS and VPC deployment.

[07:50] Liam: on pricing we also need clarity on how embeddings and rerank calls bill — our workflow uses embeddings heavily for retrieval.

[07:58] Maya: embeddings are billed per vector generation token and have their own pricing tiers; batching and caching apply differently — vector caching is possible if you dedupe inputs. we'll include embeddings line items in the spreadsheet.

[08:12] Ethan: any gotchas we should watch for in terms of hidden costs? e.g., data egress, storage for KV caches, logging retention?

[08:22] Luis: good question. egress for private deployments depends on cloud region and customer's network; hosted has standard egress pricing. storage for cache is usually minor compared to GPU costs but if you retain long histories that adds storage/replication cost. logging retention beyond standard retention windows is an add-on. we'll call these out in the cost model.

[08:40] Priya: about quantization — do you have recommended quant levels and how much complexity to expect in switching?

[08:47] Maya: we typically recommend 4-bit or 8-bit quant for inference where supported. 4-bit can reduce memory footprint significantly and increase throughput but requires validation for quality on your prompts. switching can be a config + redeploy of model artifact; our team can manage the conversion and can show AB test results.

[09:05] Ethan: what's the expected timeline from pilot -> prod if we go with dedicated?

[09:12] Jordan: pilot + benchmark: 2-4 weeks. onboarding dedicated capacity and deploying models post-pilot is typically 4-8 weeks depending on network/VPC needs and any compliance gating. private/on-prem can be longer.

[09:25] Liam: procurement question — do you support PO-based billing and net-30?

[09:30] Jordan: yes, for enterprise deals we support PO and net-30 terms; committed contracts have standard enterprise invoicing.

[09:36] Sara: one last point — we run in multiple regions, any constraints on model availability and latency across regions?

[09:43] Luis: we operate regional pools; some model variants may not be in every region immediately, but we can replicate or route to nearby pools. that can affect latency for certain geos so we'll call that out.

[09:58] Ethan: great. let's recap next steps.

[10:02] Jordan: recap — Jordan to send detailed cost spreadsheet and hosted vs dedicated scenarios; Maya to set up benchmark plan and schedule the deep-dive; Priya to send sample prompt/token histograms; Sara to coordinate security docs exchange. We'll aim to have pricing and pilot plan by end of next week.

[10:20] Liam: sounds good. thanks everyone.

[10:24] Jordan: thanks all, we'll follow up in email with links to the docs and the spreadsheet.

Notes: transcription includes occasional mis-hearings ("K-V cash" for KV cache), filler words, and speaker overlaps. Links shared during call: (1) Redwood pricing overview (link), (2) sample benchmark template (link), (3) SOC2 summary doc (link).

End of transcript.
